source.title: BENCH-SPACE-004: quantify supplier concentration versus cislunar service resilience
source.body:
## Research basis

The OECD's 2026 Space Economy at a Glance assesses a space economy whose access has broadened while launch activity, orbital infrastructure and supply chains remain concentrated. It reports that four providers accounted for more than four-fifths of orbital launches in 2025 in one commonly used metric and highlights single-country dependencies in crucial space-related inputs. See https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-space-economy-at-a-glance-2026_cbf9b240-en/full-report/managing-vulnerabilities-dependencies-and-sustainability-risks-of-the-space-economy_4d97ef6d.html

These real-world observations motivate this benchmark; the fixture values below are synthetic and must not be presented as the OECD's provider shares or as an actual procurement dataset.

## Paradigm shift

Treat supplier diversity as a measurable resilience attribute with an explicit cost—not as a slogan and not as a proxy for arbitrary failure probabilities. Compare the cost of a concentrated procurement portfolio with the additional cost of a portfolio that can still meet its service floor after any one supplier fails.

## Synthetic reference case

Required service demand: 70 normalized capacity units.

- Concentrated portfolio capacities: 50, 20, 15, 15 (total 100); listed lifecycle procurement cost: 100 synthetic cost units; portfolio HHI: 3,350 using the sum of squared percentage shares.
- Diversified portfolio capacities: 25, 25, 25, 25 (total 100); listed lifecycle procurement cost: 118 synthetic cost units; portfolio HHI: 2,500.
- Under concentrated sourcing, losing the 50-unit provider leaves 50, below the demand floor of 70 (shortfall 20). Losing any smaller provider leaves at least 80.
- Under diversified sourcing, losing any one 25-unit provider leaves 75, satisfying demand 70.

The 18% diversification premium is the explicit trade-off in the toy case, not a real cost estimate. Deterministic fault cases do not imply that outages are equally likely or independent.

## Required invariants

1. Compute HHI from the fixture's declared capacity shares; require shares to be non-negative and sum exactly to 100% (or use an explicitly documented normalized unit).
2. Run every single-supplier failure as a separate deterministic case; do not assign outage probabilities without evidence.
3. Calculate remaining capacity, unmet demand, lifecycle cost and the service-floor result for every case.
4. If N-1 supplier resilience is a hard requirement, mark the concentrated option infeasible before ranking price; select the cheapest feasible option only after gates.
5. Report cost, HHI, capacity and service separately—no composite score may hide a hard shortfall.
6. A higher HHI is not itself proof of market power or a causal failure probability; this is a procurement exposure metric over the specified candidate portfolio.
7. Reject a claimed robust portfolio if demand is raised above the remaining capacity after its weakest single-supplier failure.

## Acceptance targets

- 100% of named single-supplier fault cases have an independently recomputed remaining-capacity result.
- Zero infeasible options may win a hard N-1 gate on the basis of lower price.
- Exact HHI outputs match the analytical oracle (3,350 and 2,500 for the frozen fixture).
- Zero probabilistic-risk claim from deterministic fault coverage.
- Reports show diversification premium, capacity shortfall and HHI side-by-side.

## Composition

This is a new synthetic portfolio slice linked to the [Space Economy Reference Benchmark Suite PR #1736](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/pull/1736) and the [common-cause resilience work #1749](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/issues/1749). It should compose with Symtropy's deterministic market/logistics models and Mycelix provenance, with Symthaea comparing policies and Sol Atlas projecting supply and dependency context. It is not a second generic market engine.
